Think of type annotations as labels you stick on a function's input slots and output tray. Python ignores the labels when it runs your code, but a type checker reads them and tells you if you're trying to put a square peg in a round hole.

cards.teaser: `Optional[X]` means a value is either `X` or `None` — the most common annotation mistake is forgetting `None` can flow in. `Union[X, Y]` generalizes this to any set of types, and Python 3.10+ lets you write both as `X | None` and `X | Y`.

Optional[str] is just shorthand for 'this slot can hold a string or nothing at all.' The type checker then acts like a strict bouncer: it won't let you use the value as a string until you've proven it isn't None.

cards.title: mypy Static Type Checker
cards.teaser: mypy reads your Python source and its type annotations, builds a model of every variable's type, and reports inconsistencies — all without running the code. It's the reference implementation of PEP 484 and the industry default for Python static analysis.

cards.title: typing.Protocol for Structural Subtyping
cards.teaser: `Protocol` lets you define an interface by the methods an object must have, not by the class it must inherit from. Any class with the right method signatures satisfies the protocol — no registration, no explicit `implements` keyword needed.

A Protocol is a checklist of methods. Any object that checks all the boxes qualifies, regardless of its family tree. You're describing what something can do, not what it is.

cards.title: TypeAlias for Type Aliases
cards.teaser: `TypeAlias` explicitly declares that a name is a type alias, not a variable assignment. This makes long complex types readable and communicates intent to both humans and type checkers — especially important when an alias is shared across modules.

A TypeAlias is a nickname for a type. Instead of writing the full complex type every time, you give it a short meaningful name and use that name everywhere. TypeAlias just tells the type checker 'this name is a nickname, not a regular variable.'

cards.title: cast() for Type Narrowing

cards.title: TYPE_CHECKING for Import-Time Types
cards.teaser: `TYPE_CHECKING` is a constant that is `False` at runtime but `True` when a type checker analyzes your code. Wrapping imports inside `if TYPE_CHECKING:` eliminates circular imports and avoids loading heavy modules that are only needed for annotations.

runs.text: Large codebases frequently hit circular import problems: module A imports module B for type annotations, and module B imports module A for something real.

cards.title: @overload for Function Overloads

cards.title: Gradual Typing Philosophy
cards.teaser: Gradual typing lets you add annotations incrementally — unannotated code is treated as `Any` (fully permissive) while annotated code is strictly checked. You can add type safety one module at a time without annotating everything at once.

runs.text: as Python's answer to the annotation dilemma: you shouldn't have to annotate everything or nothing.

is compatible with every other type in both directions. Unannotated functions implicitly use
for every parameter and return type.

The strategy for annotating a legacy codebase: start at the leaves (utility functions with no dependencies), annotate their signatures, run mypy to catch immediate errors, then work inward toward the core. Each annotated module becomes a typed island that interacts safely with the surrounding untyped sea.

runs.text: Gradual typing is not 'optional types.' It is a formal system where
plays a precise role: it is both a subtype and a supertype of every other type, acting as a bridge between typed and untyped worlds without breaking the type algebra.

Gradual typing is like adding guardrails to a road one section at a time. The sections with guardrails are safe; the sections without are as risky as before. You add safety incrementally without having to redo the entire road at once.
